videos.script: For years, putting three boxes side by side in CSS was a trick. Floats, inline blocks, tables. Each one worked until it did not. {{row}} Flexbox is the answer that was designed for the job. You write display flex on a container, and its children line up in a row. {{axes}} Everything else in Flexbox follows from one idea: two axes. The main axis is the direction the items line up in. The cross axis runs across it. One property places items along the main axis. Another places them across. {{space}} Then there is the space that is left over. A row of three books on a shelf six hundred pixels wide leaves room to spare. Flexbox can push them together, spread them out, or grow them to fill it. You will measure every one of those choices. {{grow}} Growing is where the arithmetic is. Flex grow does not share out the width. It shares out what is left, and you will see the difference in the numbers. {{trap}} And there is one trap that catches everyone, a long word that refuses to shrink. {{end}} At the end, the patterns you will build again and again. A menu in a row. Something centred, both ways. A footer that stays at the bottom. {{close}}
